92.title: Janmashtami: the girl in the cell
92.hook: the baby girl left in Kamsa's cell rises as the Goddess: the Lord's hidden power, revealed
92.carry: yogamaya: god hides in plain sight
92.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, then celebrate Krishna's birth with songs and by rocking a small cradle with an image of baby Krishna; the next day, especially in Maharashtra, teams form human pyramids to break a high-hung pot of curd, called dahi handi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rakhi and its promise of protection. Today, back to the prison on Janmashtami night, and the baby girl left in the cell.

Midnight in King Kamsa's prison. Krishna is born, the guards asleep, the chains loose, and Vasudeva carries the baby through the storm and across the Yamuna to the cowherd village. In Yashoda's house he leaves his son, picks up her newborn daughter, and carries her back through the rain. By morning he's in his cell again, chains on, as if nothing happened. The guards wake to the sound of a baby crying. They run to tell the king. And Kamsa comes down the stairs to the prison, for the eighth child.
screen: `THE SWAP IN THE NIGHT.` → `A BABY CRYING IN THE CELL.` → `KAMSA COMES DOWN THE STAIRS.`

segments.voice: Devaki begs him. It's a girl, she says. How could a little girl harm you? Let me keep just this one. Kamsa doesn't listen. The Bhagavata Purana says he seizes the baby by the feet and swings her to dash her against a stone. She slips out of his hands. She rises into the air, and in the sky she's no longer a baby. She's the Goddess, shining, with eight arms and weapons in every hand: Yogamaya, the power of the Lord's own mystery. It was her power, the Bhagavata says, that put the guards to sleep, and she had been born as Yashoda's daughter to make the whole rescue possible. She speaks to Kamsa from the sky: the one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Then she's gone. Now the teaching inside this night. Yogamaya is God's power to hide, and to work while hidden. Krishna himself later says he isn't revealed to everyone, because he's veiled by his yogamaya. Look at how God arrives here. Not with thunder. Carried through the rain in a basket, raised as a cowherd's boy, while the Goddess lies in a prison cell disguised as a baby girl nobody wanted. Many Hindus take this to heart: God often works hidden, through ordinary people and ordinary things, and the one everyone overlooks may be the holiest one in the room. It's part of why, at midnight, many families rock a little cradle with baby Krishna in it. The Lord of the universe, small enough to hold. Yogamaya: God hides in plain sight.
screen: `SHE SLIPS OUT OF HIS HANDS.` · `YOGAMAYA, THE GODDESS, IN THE SKY.` · `GOD WORKS HIDDEN.` · `A CRADLE AT MIDNIGHT.` · then, large: `YOGAMAYA: GOD HIDES IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you pray, picture the little cradle at midnight, or rock one if your family keeps it, and say softly, Jai Shri Krishna. Stay a moment with God made small enough to hold. If you don't pray, think of someone you usually overlook, at home, at school, at work, and wonder, just for a minute, what you haven't seen in them. Sit with that, and wait in the dark.
Janmashtami. The birth on the eighth night, and a rescue worked in secret by the Lord's own mystery.
Your line: yogamaya: god hides in plain sight. Even in a baby girl in a prison cell. Ninety-two days, and counting.

93.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: Ganpati Bappa Morya
93.hook: an old devotee who can't walk to the temple anymore, and why the crowds shout his name with Ganesha's
93.carry: bhakti: god walks toward you too
93.howItsDone: During Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindu families bring a clay Ganesha home as a guest for a day and a half up to ten days, and at the immersion, especially in Maharashtra, crowds shout 'Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya': come back soon next year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami, and yogamaya: God hiding in plain sight, even in a baby girl. Today, Ganesha comes home again, and a chant with a man's name in it.

The last day of Ganesh Chaturthi in Pune or Mumbai. The clay Ganesha is lifted onto a cart, the drums start, and the whole street walks him to the water, shouting one line over and over: Ganpati Bappa Morya! Bappa is Marathi for father. So the crowd is calling God Dad. But who is Morya? He isn't a god. He was a man, a devotee, and huge crowds shout his name with Ganesha's every year. Here's how that happened.
screen: `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA!` → `BAPPA MEANS FATHER.` → `SO WHO IS MORYA?`

segments.voice: Morya Gosavi lived centuries ago near Pune, and he loved Ganesha. As the Chinchwad tradition tells it, every month he walked from his home at Chinchwad to Ganesha's temple at Morgaon, a long way on foot, year after year. Then he grew old, and the walk became too much. He was heartbroken. What is a devotee who can't reach the temple anymore? The tradition says Ganesha came to him in a dream: don't worry. I'll come to you. Soon after, bathing in the river at Morgaon, Morya found a small stone image of Ganesha in the water, carried it home to Chinchwad, and built a temple for it there. The devotee couldn't make the journey, so God made it instead. People say Morya's love was so complete that his name and Ganesha's became one cry: Ganpati Bappa Morya. That's the teaching inside the chant. In bhakti, the path of loving devotion, the love runs both ways. The devotee walks toward God, and God walks toward the devotee. Close enough to call Bappa, Dad. Close enough that a devotee's name gets shouted with his. And it's why Ganesh Chaturthi works the way it does. Families don't only go to the temple; they bring Ganesha home as a guest, for a day and a half, or five days, or ten. Then at the water they shout the rest of the line, in Marathi: pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Come back soon next year. You don't say that to a distant god. You say it to someone who has come to your house, and who you know will come again. Bhakti: God walks toward you too.
screen: `THE LONG WALK TO MORGAON.` · `DON'T WORRY. I'LL COME TO YOU.` · `THE LOVE RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · `GANESHA COMES HOME AS A GUEST.` · then, large: `BHAKTI: GOD WALKS TOWARD YOU TOO.`

segments.voice: If you pray, picture Ganesha arriving at your door the way families welcome him, with drums and flowers, and say softly, three times: Ganpati Bappa Morya. Then, before you open your eyes, say the second half: come back soon. If you don't pray, think of someone who came to you when you couldn't get to them, and say their name, with thanks. Breathe, and let them in.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's festival on the fourth day, when he comes home as a guest, and the crowds call him Bappa.

94.title: Navaratri: Rama wakes the Goddess
94.hook: before his last battle Rama wakes the Goddess out of season, and offers his own eye when one lotus goes missing
94.carry: shakti first: even rama asked the mother
94.howItsDone: Hindus keep Navaratri in many regional ways: honoring a form of the Goddess each night (the Navadurga), garba dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, golu dolls in the south, and Ramlila plays in the north ending on Dussehra, when effigies of Ravana are burned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi, and Morya, the devotee God walked toward. Today, the nine nights again, and a prince who needed the Goddess before his biggest fight.

Rama has an army, a bridge across the sea, and Hanuman. Sita is across the water in Lanka. And Ravana still can't be beaten. In the Bengali telling of the Ramayana, by the poet Krittivasa, Rama sees he can't win alone. He needs the Goddess. But it's autumn, and in the old reckoning this is the gods' night, their half of the year for sleeping. So Rama does what no one had done before. He wakes the Goddess out of season.
screen: `SITA IS ACROSS THE SEA.` → `RAMA CAN'T WIN ALONE.` → `WAKING THE GODDESS OUT OF SEASON.`

segments.voice: It's called akal bodhan, the untimely awakening. Rama sets up an image of Durga and worships her with everything he has. For the last offering he needs a hundred and eight blue lotuses, and Hanuman flies off and brings them. Rama offers them one by one, a prayer with each. At the very end, his hand finds nothing. One lotus is missing. In the telling, the Goddess herself has hidden it, to test him. And Rama remembers what people call him: the lotus-eyed one. He takes up an arrow to offer one of his own eyes as the last lotus. Before he can, Durga appears, stops his hand, and blesses him. Then the war, and Ravana falls; many Hindus remember his fall on the tenth day. That's why Bengal keeps its great Durga Puja in autumn, and why the tenth day, Vijayadashami, holds two victories: Durga's over the buffalo demon, and Rama's over Ravana. Now the teaching. For many Hindus, Rama is God himself, born as a prince. And even he bows to the Goddess before the battle. Many Hindus, especially those who worship the Goddess, teach that Shakti, the Mother's power, is what makes every action possible, even God's. So before the hard thing, you go to her. That's what the nine nights are for many families: nine forms of the Goddess, the Navadurga, one honored each night, from Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain, to Siddhidatri, giver of perfection. And notice what Rama offered. Not gold. Himself, holding nothing back. Shakti first: even Rama asked the Mother.

segments.voice: Name one hard thing coming up this week. If you pray, light a lamp or picture one, and say Jai Mata Di, or a Durga prayer you know, and ask the Mother for strength before you start, the way Rama did. If you don't pray, name the hard thing, then name one person whose strength you'd borrow for it. Three slow breaths, then rest.

95.title: The question about caste
95.hook: a boy who tells a teacher the plain truth about not knowing his father, and the question a classmate asks today
95.carry: satya: the door opened for truth, not birth
95.howItsDone: Hindus hold many views on caste: many reject ranking by birth outright, some read varna as temperament and calling, and families and teachers differ; untouchability is abolished by India's constitution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri, and Rama asking the Mother first. Today, a harder question, one a lot of Hindu kids get asked at school.

A boy wants to study with a famous teacher, and the first thing a teacher will ask is his family line. So he goes to his mother: who is my father? Her answer is brave. When she was young, she says, she worked as a servant, moving from house to house, and she doesn't know. Tell him you're Satyakama, son of Jabala. So the boy walks to the teacher's door and says exactly that. And everyone waits to see if the door shuts. A version of that moment still happens, in a classroom, when someone asks: isn't Hinduism just the caste system?
screen: `WHO IS MY FATHER?` → `SAY EXACTLY THAT.` → `ISN'T HINDUISM JUST CASTE?`

segments.voice: Here's how the old story ends. The teacher listens and says: only a true brahmin would speak such truth. Bring the firewood; I'll teach you. One of the oldest Upanishads tells it; people have argued about it since. Some hear birth being set aside for honesty. Others notice the teacher still reaches for the old label. Both readings are honest. Now the hard part, plainly. The English word caste comes from Portuguese, casta, a lineage. It lumps together two Indian ideas. Varna is the four classes the old texts describe: priests and teachers, rulers and warriors, traders and farmers, and workers. In the Gita, Krishna says the four were made by quality and action. Jati means birth, and it's the word for the thousands of communities people are actually born into. Over centuries, birth won. Families were ranked, some people were treated as untouchable, and real harm was done, and in places it still is. Many Hindus pushed back, too. The poet-saint Ravidas, a leatherworker by trade, is still sung and honored. B. R. Ambedkar, born into a family treated as untouchable, fought caste fiercely and helped write India's constitution, which abolished untouchability. Hindus today still disagree about what varna was ever meant to be, and your family and your teachers may see it differently. So what do you say in the classroom? Something true. Caste is real, it hurt people, and many Hindus reject ranking anyone by birth. Then say what you stand for. Satyakama got through the door with one thing: satya, truth. Start there.
screen: `ONLY A TRUE BRAHMIN SPEAKS SUCH TRUTH.` · `VARNA AND JATI, TWO IDEAS.` · `BIRTH WON, AND PEOPLE WERE HURT.` · `SAY WHAT'S TRUE, THEN WHAT YOU STAND FOR.` · then, large: `THE DOOR OPENED FOR TRUTH.`

segments.voice: First, a time someone decided who you were before you spoke, by your name, your accent, your skin, your family; feel how small that box was. Then, if one comes, a time you did the same to someone else; no need to punish yourself, just see it. Satyakama walked to the teacher's door with nothing but the truth; let that be enough for this sit.
Jati. Birth: the community a person is born into, and most of what people mean by caste.

96.title: Holi: love without a body
96.hook: Shiva's third eye burns the god of love to ash, and love lives on without a body
96.carry: kama: love is an aim of life, within dharma
96.howItsDone: In parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, the Holi full moon is kept as Kama Dahanam, remembering Kama burned by Shiva's third eye, with bonfires and songs; across India, the day after the full moon is kept with colors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jati, the question about caste, and Satyakama telling the plain truth. Today, one more fire, and the last of the stories for now.
screen: `SATYA: THE DOOR OPENED FOR TRUTH, NOT BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Shiva sits in meditation on a mountain, so deep and so still that nothing reaches him. He's been there since his first wife, Sati, died. The gods need him to wake up, to marry again, to have a son who can defeat a demon. So they send the god of love, Kama, with his bow of sugarcane and his arrows of flowers, to shoot one into Shiva's heart. You've met Prahlad walking out of the fire, and Krishna coloring Radha's face in Braj. This is Holi's third story, and in parts of south India it's the one told at Holi's full moon.
screen: `SHIVA, STILL AS A MOUNTAIN.` → `KAMA DRAWS HIS FLOWER BOW.` → `HOLI'S THIRD STORY.`

segments.voice: Kama shoots. The arrow lands. And Shiva opens his third eye. Fire pours out of it, and Kama is burned to ash where he stands. His wife, Rati, falls weeping on the ashes. Here the story turns. Shiva, moved, promises that Kama will live again, but without a body. Love, from now on, will be everywhere and visible nowhere. That's why one of Kama's names is Ananga, the bodiless one. And Shiva does wake, and does marry Parvati. In parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, Holi's full moon is remembered as Kama Dahanam, the burning of Kama, with fires and songs of Rati's grief. Now the teaching. You might expect a god of ascetics to end love for good. The tradition doesn't. Kama, love, desire and enjoyment, is one of the four aims of a human life that Hinduism names: dharma, doing right; artha, making a living; kama, love and pleasure; and moksha, freedom. Love isn't the enemy. It's one of the goals. But it isn't the boss, either. Kama is meant to be held inside dharma. Many teachers read Shiva's fire that way: love that barges in uninvited gets burned, and love that serves the right thing, here a marriage the whole world needed, is given back and set loose everywhere. Then comes Holi morning, and the colors. And that's the last of the stories, for now. Tomorrow the path turns to practice: breath, mantra, a home shrine. The stories come with you. Kama: love is an aim of life, within dharma.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a love in your life: a person, a place, something you enjoy. In Hindu teaching it's nothing to be ashamed of; it's one of life's aims. Now ask it one honest question: does this love sit inside doing right, or is it pushing dharma out of the way? If you pray, offer that love to God and ask that it serve what's right. Then breathe, and let yourself be glad of it.
Holi. The festival of colors, the morning after the fire, where Prahlad, Radha and Kama all have a story.
Your line: kama: love is an aim of life, within dharma. Love got loose in the world. That's the last of the stories, for now.

97.title: The breath you already have
97.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin daily meditation or puja by sitting quietly and watching the breath for a few minutes, understood as prana, the life-force, before any breath practice or mantra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last story: Holi, Kama burned to ash, and love set loose without a body. Your line was kama: love is an aim of life, within dharma. The stories come with us; today the practices begin.
screen: `KAMA: LOVE IS AN AIM OF LIFE, WITHIN DHARMA.`

segments.voice: You've been doing it, without a break, since the second you were born. You're doing it now. All day and all night you breathe in and out, and almost none of those breaths are ones you chose. You don't decide to breathe while you sleep, or while you read this. It just happens. Camp three, the practices, starts here: less listening, more doing, and each week adds one piece to a routine that's yours. The tradition has a word for what's moving when you breathe.
screen: `SINCE THE SECOND YOU WERE BORN.` → `YOU DON'T DECIDE IT.` → `CAMP THREE: THE PRACTICES.`

segments.voice: The word is prana. It's often translated as breath, and it is breath, but it's more than air. Prana means life, the life-force, the thing moving in you as long as you're alive. The breath is where you can feel it most easily. The Upanishads tell a story about it. The senses argue about which of them is most important. Speech says: me. The eye says: me. The ear, the mind: me, me. So they agree to a test: each one leaves the body for a year. Speech leaves, and the body lives on, silent. The eye leaves, and the body lives on, blind. The ear, the mind, the same. Then breath gets ready to leave, and, the Chandogya Upanishad says, like a strong horse tearing up the pegs it's tied to, it starts to pull all the others up with it. They beg it to stay. You're the greatest, they say. Don't go. Everything else you do, you do because breath is doing its work first. So this week, pranayama, the breath practices, doesn't begin by controlling anything. It begins by noticing: watching the breath that's already here, without changing it. That's harder than it sounds, because the moment many people watch the breath, they start to fix it. Let it be the way it is. That's the teaching under the story: prana, the breath, is life itself, and every other power in you rests on it. Prana: breath is life itself.
screen: `PRANA — BREATH, AND LIFE ITSELF.` · `THE SENSES ARGUE.` · `BREATH TEARS UP THE PEGS.` · `FIRST, JUST NOTICE.` · then, large: `PRANA: BREATH IS LIFE ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, back tall but not stiff, hands resting, eyes closed or lowered, and find where you feel the breath most: the cool air at the tip of the nose, the rise of the chest, the belly moving. Pick one place and rest your attention there and watch the breath come in and go out, the way you'd watch waves, without deepening or slowing it. When your mind wanders, and it will, that's fine; notice where it went and come back to the breath; every coming back is the practice.
Prana. Breath, and the life that moves with it. The first thing the practice asks you to notice.
Your line: prana: breath is life itself. It's been holding you up all day. Day ninety-seven, done.

98.title: The mind like the wind
98.hook: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; the breath is where you can reach it
98.carry: arjuna's wind: the mind follows the breath
98.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers begin pranayama with slow, even breathing through the nose, the exhale longer than the inhale, sometimes silently repeating a name of God, teaching that a steadier breath brings a steadier mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prana: breath, and the life that moves with it. Your line was prana: breath is life itself. Today, for the first time, you change it. Gently.

A hard email, a slammed door, a long line at the pharmacy. Heart pounding, jaw tight, thoughts spinning, and somebody says: just breathe. It's annoying advice, mostly because nobody says why it would help. The tradition has an answer, and it starts with a complaint. On the battlefield, Krishna has just described a yogi sitting perfectly still, steady as a lamp out of the wind. And Arjuna pushes back: I can't do that. My mind won't hold still.
screen: `JUST BREATHE. BUT WHY?` → `ARJUNA: I CAN'T DO THAT.` → `MY MIND WON'T HOLD STILL.`

segments.voice: Arjuna doesn't hold back. The mind is restless, Krishna, he says. Stubborn, strong, it shakes me. Trying to hold it is like trying to hold the wind. And Krishna doesn't argue. Yes, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held, by practice and by letting go. Abhyasa and vairagya: practice, again and again, and loosening your grip on what pulls you away. That's in the Bhagavad Gita, and Hindu teachers have leaned on it ever since. Here's where the breath comes in. Arjuna compared the mind to wind. The old yoga manuals take that seriously: breath and mind move together. When the breath is jumpy, the mind is jumpy; when the breath grows slow and steady, the mind follows. You can't grab the wind of your thoughts. But you can reach the wind in your lungs. So pranayama, breath practice, is a doorway to the mind. Today, a first, gentle change. Breathe in through the nose for a count of four. Breathe out, through the nose if you can, for a count of six. No holding, no forcing. Many teachers call the out-breath the settling half, and you can feel why: your heart speeds up a little as you breathe in, and slows a little as you breathe out. If six strains, use three in and five out; if you get dizzy, stop and breathe normally. The count isn't a test. And when your mind blows away mid-count, that's Arjuna's wind. Come back. That's abhyasa. The mind follows the breath.
screen: `AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.` · `PRACTICE, AND LETTING GO.` · `BREATH AND MIND MOVE TOGETHER.` · `FOUR IN, SIX OUT.` · then, large: `THE MIND FOLLOWS THE BREATH.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and soft, take one ordinary breath to arrive, then breathe in through the nose for four and out slowly for six, counting quietly at whatever speed feels natural. No holding at the top or the bottom. If you pray, let each out-breath carry a name of God, like Ram, or the sound Om. When the mind drifts, that's the wind; come back. If it strains, shorten both numbers.
Out-breath, the half of the breath you lengthen: four counts in, six counts out, the first way this practice steadies the wind of the mind.
Your line: arjuna's wind: the mind follows the breath. Four in, six out, whenever the wind picks up. See you tomorrow.
